children: U.S. wheat futures rose on Monday as Black Sea attacks sparked fears of more disruption to Russian and Ukrainian exports.
Soybeans were slightly firmer and corn fell as a stronger dollar made U.S. supplies more expensive in export markets.
Chicago Board of Trade most-active wheat
rose 0.5% to $7.29-1/2 a bushel at 1134 GMT. Soybeans
Russian and Ukrainian ship-borne Black Sea exports are at a near standstill after attacks on each other's ports and shipping.

"Wheat is being strengthened today by concern about continued interruption of Russian and Ukrainian Black Sea exports by ship, with attacks continuing and no real sign of any significant peace talks," said StoneX commodity risk manager Matt Ammermann.
"There have been a lot of headlines about possible Black Sea peace initiatives but nothing concrete seems to be happening and shipping disruption continues," he said.
"Global import demand has been restrained but some wheat demand could return this week with tenders from Pakistan and Algeria," Ammermann added.
Pakistan has issued a huge tender to purchase 750,000 metric tons of wheat. Major importer Algeria wants at least 50,000 tons but generally buys more than its nominal tender volume.

Soybean strength was limited after the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) raised its soybean production forecast on Friday. The USDA also forecast a smaller U.S. corn crop but analysts had expected an even greater reduction.
Corn and soybeans are facing weakness from the stronger dollar, he said. The USDA crop forecast changes had been anticipated by the market and were met by profit-taking.
"Falls in soybeans are limited by expectations of more Chinese buying of U.S. beans ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping's upcoming visit to Washington," he said.
